rationale.rationale: Management frames the separation as two linked moves to unwind a conglomerate structure in which crop protection and seeds compete for the same capital. On the Feb 2, 2026 call, Toshan Tamhane gave three objectives for the Advanta (seeds) IPO: (a) deleveraging of UPL Ltd's balance sheet, (b) value unlock for KKR, which put in a cheque of '$300-plus million' into Advanta more than three years earlier, and (c) the argument that 'the needs of crop protection in terms of the cash flows, capital allocation are very different from that of the seeds business,' citing Corteva's own announced split of crop protection and seeds as validation, and describing Advanta as the eighth largest seeds player globally with 'a journey and destiny of its own.' Bikash Prasad stressed the Advanta listing is an offer for sale, not a primary raise — Advanta is cash-surplus and does not need the money — with proceeds going to the group 'largely for deleveraging of the group balance sheet,' and valuation to be set by a book-building price discovery process under applicable law. The separately filed Scheme (board-approved February 20, 2026) then consolidates the India crop protection business held in UPL SAS (UPL holds 90.91%) and the international crop protection business held via UPL Corp / UPL Cayman (UPL holds 77.78%) into UPL Global ('UPL 2'), to be listed — billed as the 'World's Second Largest Listed Pure-Play Crop Protection Platform' — via amalgamation of UPL SAS into UPL, a vertical demerger of India crop protection into UPL Global, and amalgamation of UPL Corp into UPL Global, with no cash consideration. The stated problems it solves: a complicated group structure with misaligned shareholder interests across layered subsidiaries, blurred value discovery for investors, constrained independent capital-raising, and split managerial and board focus; the demerged India crop protection undertaking was INR 24,120 Mn of turnover in FY25, 31.15% of combined UPL 1 turnover. Ratios: 1,000 UPL 1 shares (INR 2) for every 48 UPL SAS shares (INR 10); 1,000 UPL 2 shares for every 213 UPL Cayman shares (USD 1); and 1:1 UPL 2 for UPL 1 on the demerger, leaving UPL 1 promoters at 33.09% (from 33.51%) and UPL 2 at 71.56% promoter / 28.44% public. On the call an analyst (Tarang) pushed back hard that deleveraging and an exit for an external shareholder make sense but value creation for a UPL minority shareholder does not, given how the entities are stacked — a challenge management did not rebut.
rationale.evolution: The passages supplied are all tagged [Feb 2026], so the three-year arc is not visible in them; within that window the sequence is a Q3 FY26 earnings call where the Advanta seeds IPO was raised only in Q&A, under analyst questioning, and was defended as an offer for sale for group deleveraging plus a KKR exit, with the crop-protection-versus-seeds capital allocation logic offered last ('And lastly, third...'). Management there pointed outward to Corteva's announced crop protection/seeds split rather than to a UPL plan of its own, and declined to discuss Advanta's valuation beyond saying the Board would assess market conditions at the time. Weeks later, on February 20, 2026, the Board formalised the far larger step in a composite scheme of arrangement creating a separately listed pure-play crop protection entity (UPL Global), where the rationale shifts from deleveraging and partner exit to structural simplification, clearer value discovery and independent capital raising. So the idea moves from a cash-raising/partner-exit transaction at the seeds subsidiary to a full two-listed-entity reorganisation of the parent.

points.point: CFO Bikash Prasad confirmed the Advanta IPO is secondary, not a primary raise — no new money into Advanta.
points.quote: So this transaction is offer for sale. It's not a primary transaction.

points.point: Proceeds are earmarked for the group's balance sheet rather than business investment.
points.quote: he group largely for deleveraging of the group balance sheet.

points.point: Asked whether it is essentially deleveraging plus an exit for external shareholders, management conceded that is how it looks as of now, subject to market conditions and a final Board assessment.
points.quote: But yes, largely, we can say as we think now, it looks like more for deleveraging.

points.point: Toshan Tamhane set out three objectives, the first two being UPL deleveraging and value unlock for KKR, which invested over $300 million into Advanta more than three years earlier.
points.quote: There is b ) value unlock for KKR. If you recollect KKR partnered with Advanta more than 3 years back when they put in a check of $300 -plus million into Advanta.

points.point: The third objective is the structural argument: seeds and crop protection have fundamentally different cash flow and capital allocation needs.
points.quote: And lastly, third, we believe that the needs of crop protection in terms of the cash flows, capital allocation are very different from that of the seeds business.

points.point: Management cited Corteva's announced crop protection/seeds split as external validation and positioned Advanta as the eighth largest global seeds player deserving its own path.
points.quote: As you would have seen globally, Corteva has also announced a split between crop protection and seeds because just those two businesses are fundamentally different, and we believe Advanta as the eighth largest seeds player globally has a journey and destiny of its own.

points.point: Management said the unlocked value reaches UPL both as shareholder and through restructuring/deleveraging, with price discovery happening via the IPO.
points.quote: And that value does flow through to UPL, both as a shareholder and from a restructuring deleveraging standpoint.

points.point: The analyst's unresolved objection: the logic works for deleveraging and for the external shareholder's exit, but not evidently for a UPL minority holder given the holding structure; management did not quantify a rebuttal.
points.quote: But from being a shareholder at UPL, given the structure of how these entities are placed, I'm not too sure how much of value creation will it help for a shareholder of UPL .

points.point: The Scheme consolidates the India crop protection business in UPL SAS and the global crop protection business in UPL Cayman into one focused, pure-play platform with independent management.
points.quote: The Scheme proposes to consolidate  the India Crop Protection Business held in UPL SAS and Global Crop Protection Business held in UPL Cayman, under a single entity, creating a focused, pure-play crop protection platform.

points.point: Two listed entities result: UPL 1 as a diversified agriculture and specialty chemicals platform that also incubates new verticals, and UPL 2 as a dedicated crop protection platform, so investors can self-select by strategy and risk profile.
points.quote: This will enable clearer value discovery by providing flexibility to the investors to select investments which best suit their investment strategies and risk profile.

points.point: Each entity gains independent access to capital and can optimise its own capital structure, aligning capital allocation to focused strategies.
points.quote: The Scheme will allow UPL 1 and UPL 2 to raise capital independently, allowing each entity to optimize its capital structure and pursue business opportunities more efficiently and effectively.

points.point: Structural simplification is an explicit goal — aligning operations and the interests of different shareholder groups across the layered holding chain — plus manufacturing and market-access synergies and cost efficiencies.
points.quote: The Scheme will simplify the group structure by aligning business operations and interests of various shareholders.

points.point: The filing names the constituencies being courted: a different set of investors, strategic partners and lenders, alongside sharper managerial and board focus.
points.quote: The Scheme will e nhance managerial and board focus and enable UPL 2 to build a wider capital and financial base, by attracting a different set of investors, strategic partners, lenders and stakeholders, as well as promoting overall business growth .

points.point: Scale framing: the press release headlines the creation of the world's second largest listed pure-play crop protection platform, approved by the Board on February 20, 2026.
points.quote: UPL Announces the Creation of  World's Second Largest Listed Pure -Play Crop Protection Platform

points.point: Sizing of the demerged piece: the India crop protection undertaking had FY25 turnover of INR 24,120 Mn, 31.15% of combined UPL 1 turnover; no cash consideration is payable and UPL SAS and UPL Cayman are both dissolved.
points.quote: No cash consideration shall be payable under the Scheme.

rationale.what_management_expects: For UPL 1: a diversified agri and specialty chemicals platform incubating new verticals, de-levered by Advanta IPO proceeds. For UPL 2/UPL Global: a pure-play, independently managed crop protection platform with research, manufacturing and market-access synergies, cost efficiencies, its own optimised capital structure, and a wider base of investors, strategic partners and lenders. Across both: clearer value discovery, sharper board focus, sustainable growth.
rationale.gaps: No debt quantum or leverage target, no segment margins or synergy figures, no debt split between entities, no Advanta IPO size/valuation, timeline, tax or cost detail.

rationale.rationale: NATCO Pharma is demerging its Agrochemicals / Crop Health Sciences business (the 'Demerged Undertaking') out of the listed pharma company into Natco Crop Health Sciences Limited (the 'Resulting Company'), to be listed on BSE and NSE. The scheme's stated core reason is that the risk and reward profiles of the two verticals — Pharmaceutical and Agrochemicals — are different, so segregating them gives management better and more efficient control and a concentrated approach to each. On the calls management gave the commercial version of this: the crop business is tiny inside Natco (turnover of ₹60,62,03,918 as on 31st March 2025, just 1.48% of company turnover) and therefore 'not being valued in our system' next to a very large pharma business, so a separate listing creates visibility and value unlocking plus a 'complete see-through' into crop and pharma separately. Management said the crop business is only now about breaking even, and that as a standalone listed entity it can raise its own capital and grow by itself. In the May/Jun 2026 call the operating logic was added: the customers of the two businesses are quite different, so the demerger gives a more focused approach, and crop sales had grown to ~₹140 crore from ~₹60 crore declared the prior year, with growth to come from products, channel partners (still fewer than peers) and people additions — 'one of the main reasons for demerging and having more focus on the business.' Natco will retain about 20% of the post-listing shareholding to keep supporting a business still at early growth stages and to monitor progress and provide strategic support, with shareholders getting 1 share of ₹2 in the Resulting Company for every 1 share of ₹2 held, so they hold ~80% directly and 100% of the ultimate economic interest. The scheme also cites operational rationalization, ability to leverage each business's financial and operational resources, and letting each attract different sets of investors, strategic partners and lenders. The plan was then deferred: after the Board approved a rights issue of up to ₹1,300 crore on September 9, 2026, the Company said the resulting change to capital structure requires consequential changes to the Scheme, which has received exchange Observation Letters but has not yet been filed with the NCLT.
rationale.evolution: On the Nov 14, 2025 call the demerger surfaced in answer to investor 'Guru', who asked about value unlocking in the ROW business / agro diversification; Rajeev Nannapaneni confirmed the demerger was already announced, that the entity would list 'maybe sometime in 2026 once all the clearances come through', and that shareholders would be 'duly rewarded'. By the May 29, 2026 call (Jun 2026 tag) it had moved from announcement to execution — Rajesh Chebiyam, answering individual investor Neeraj Kayal, said the business was 'in the process of demerging', framing it around different customers, a differentiated/patent-controlled product approach, and scale-up from ~₹60 crore to ~₹140 crore of sales. The Scheme filing then formalised the rationale (different risk-reward, 1.48% of turnover, 1:1 swap, 20% retained stake, BSE/NSE listing), and the September 9, 2026 board outcome pushed the timetable back: the ₹1,300 crore rights issue will change the capital structure, so a revised Scheme — keeping the same swap ratio — will be filed with the exchanges after the rights issue, and nothing has yet gone to the NCLT.

points.point: Management's stated mechanism for value unlocking: a separate listing gives the crop business special focus and the ability to raise its own capital independently of Natco.

points.point: The problem being solved is that the crop business is too small inside Natco to be valued, sitting next to a very large pharma business; demerger is meant to get it attention and a visible valuation.
points.quote: I think you will get another business which is not being valued in our system because it is of a very tiny business and a very large business in pharma.

points.point: Management characterised the crop business's current financial state as only around break-even, and said shareholders would get separate visibility into crop and pharma, with real value visible in 2026 though numbers were unpredictable.
points.quote: Value unlocking means I think what we see is this business now is about breaking even now.

points.point: Asked directly whether the demerger is a shareholder value-unlocking opportunity, Rajeev answered unequivocally yes and said shareholders would be rewarded for the demerger.
points.quote: So, this business will get more attention and I think shareholders will be duly rewarded for the fact that it has been demerged.

points.point: Rajesh Chebiyam, answering individual investor Neeraj Kayal, said the business is in the process of being demerged and gave the primary reason as a more focused approach because the two businesses' customers are quite different.

points.point: The crop business is being built on a pharma-like strategy of differentiated, unique, patent-controlled, limited-competition molecules rather than commodity agrochemicals.
points.quote: So products which could be unique, which could be patent controlled, limited competition.

points.point: Scale cited: crop sales of close to ₹140 crore for the year versus about ₹60 crore declared the previous year, with growth from product launches, channel penetration (fewer channel partners than peers) and people additions.
points.quote: So in terms of sale, let's say, this year, we ended up close to INR140 crores, right? And as opposed to a declared number for last year was about INR60 crores.

points.point: Management tied the growth confidence directly to the demerger, naming focus on the business as a main reason for separating it.
points.quote: And that's also one of the main reasons for demerging and having more focus on the business.

points.point: The formal rationale is that the Board believes the risk and reward of the Pharmaceutical and Agrochemicals verticals are different, so the Agrochemicals Undertaking is being demerged on a going-concern basis into the Resulting Company.
points.quote: The Board of Directors of the Demerged Company believe that the risk and reward associated with each of the aforesaid business verticals are different.

points.point: Size of the demerged business is quantified: Agrochemicals turnover of ₹60,62,03,918 as on 31st March 2025, equal to 1.48% of the listed company's total turnover.

points.point: Natco will keep a 20% post-listing stake because the agrochemicals business is still at early growth stages, to continue supporting it, monitor progress and provide strategic support.
points.quote: Further, the Demerged Company intends to retain the current shareholding in the Resulting Company (20% of post listing shareholding) in order to continue to offer support to the Agrochemicals Business which is still at its early growth stages and help in monitoring the progress and providing strategic support.

points.point: Segregation is expected to give management better and more efficient control of each business and promote their growth, with a concentrated development approach for each vertical.
points.quote: The demerger, transfer and vesting of the Agrochemicals Undertaking on a going concern basis to the Resulting Company would result in better and efficient control by the management for the segregated businesses and promote their growth.

points.point: Stakeholder rationale: each business can pursue independent opportunities, efficient capital allocation, and attract its own investors, strategic partners and lenders — the explicit 'who asked for it' constituency in the filing.
points.quote: Each business would be able to address independent business opportunities, pursue efficient capital allocation and attract different sets of investors, strategic partners, lenders and other stakeholders.

points.point: Stated benefits also include focused growth, operational efficiencies, business synergies, customer focus, operational rationalization, organizational efficiency, optimum resource utilization, and explicit value unlocking of the verticals.
points.quote: The segregation is also expected to unlock the value of the business verticals of the Demerged Company.

points.point: Consideration is a 1:1 share swap (one ₹2 share of the Resulting Company per ₹2 share held), no cash, leaving shareholders ~80% direct and 100% of ultimate beneficial economic interest; listing sought on BSE and NSE.
points.quote: Overall, the shareholders of the Demerged Company will hold 100% of the ultimate beneficial economic interest in the Agrochemicals Undertaking (direct holding of about 80% and indirect holding of about 20% through the Demerged Company).

points.point: Timeline change: the ₹1,300 crore rights issue approved on September 9, 2026 will alter capital structure and shareholding, so the Scheme must be amended and refiled with the exchanges after the rights issue, with the swap ratio kept unchanged.
points.quote: The fund raising by way of a Rights Issue proposed at the meeting of the board of directors held on September 09, 2026  is expected to result in change to the Company's  capital structure and shareholding pattern and consequently would require necessary changes to the Scheme.

points.point: Procedural status: Observation Letters have been received from both stock exchanges, but the Scheme and related applications have not yet been filed with the NCLT.
points.quote: The Company has not filed the Scheme and related applications with the Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal.

rationale.rationale: Astral Limited says it has grown into two distinct verticals — (a) Plumbing: pipes, fittings, water tanks, faucets and sanitaryware, and (b) Chemicals: adhesives, polyvinyl acetate (PVA), cyanoacrylates, solvent cements, silicone sealants, epoxy resins, construction chemicals, putties and allied products, further scaled into specialty chemicals through recent strategic acquisitions. The Board (approval dated June 25, 2026) adopted a Composite Scheme that (i) demerges the Chemicals/Chemical Undertaking of Astral Limited (the Demerged Company) on a going-concern basis into Astral Chemie Limited, formerly Astral Coatings Private Limited, a 100% subsidiary that already manufactures and supplies paints and coatings for residential, commercial and industrial end-users, and (ii) amalgamates Al-Aziz Plastics Private Limited, another 100% subsidiary making electrofusion fittings, compression fittings, saddles, electrical fittings and allied accessories for gas, water, electricity and solar distribution/transmission, into Astral Limited because it is complementary to the Plumbing Business. The size cited: the Demerged Undertaking's turnover for the year ended March 31, 2026 was ₹12,663 million, 21% of the Demerged Company's total turnover, against Astral Limited's standalone FY26 turnover of ₹59,076 million and net worth of ₹41,058 million; Al-Aziz was small at ₹373 million turnover and ₹215 million net worth. The stated problems it solves: each business has different products, customer segments, operating models, capital requirements, risk profiles and growth opportunities and operates under different macroeconomic environments, regulatory frameworks and market risks, so one corporate roof blurred focus — the demerger puts chemicals plus paints under a single dedicated platform run by a focused leadership team with deep sector-specific expertise, and isolates the operational, cyclical and compliance risks of each business. It is also framed as a capital-structure fix: each entity can independently determine capex, working capital, funding and investment strategy based on its own growth prospects, capital intensity, cash-flow profile and risk-return characteristics, and as separately listed entities both can independently access debt and equity capital and attract strategic and financial investors with different investment objectives. For Al-Aziz, the added reasons are integration of its manufacturing facilities, products and customer relationships with Plumbing, plus reduced legal and regulatory compliance burden and administrative costs. Mechanics are value-neutral to holders: no cash consideration, 1 equity share of Astral Chemie (₹1 face value) for every 1 Astral share (₹1 face value), a mirrored shareholding pattern (promoters 54.22%, public 45.78% post-Scheme versus 100% promoter-held pre-Scheme), Astral's existing shares in Astral Chemie cancelled, no change in Astral's own shareholding, and listing sought on NSE and BSE.
rationale.evolution: The reasoning cannot be traced call by call from the material supplied: the only earnings-call passage provided is [May 2025], and it is entirely about end-market sizing — PVC at about 4.5 million tons in fiscal 25, CPVC at roughly 2.5 lakh tons or about 5% of PVC, and fire-sprinkler pipes as the next leg of CPVC demand — with no mention of a demerger, of the chemicals vertical, or of Astral Coatings/Astral Chemie. The separation therefore appears in these texts only at the Board approval of the Composite Scheme on June 25, 2026, sized off FY26 (year ended March 31, 2026) financials, by which point Astral Coatings Private Limited had already been renamed Astral Chemie Limited and the chemicals portfolio had been expanded 'through recent strategic acquisitions' into specialty chemicals — the one hint of a build-up preceding the announcement. One drafting shift is visible inside the filing itself: the rationale annexure and disclosure tables describe the demerger of the 'Chemical Undertaking'/'Chemicals Business Undertaking', while the press-release text describes 'the demerger of its Adhesive Business', a narrower label for the same undertaking.

points.point: Management sized CPVC at about 2.5 lakh tonnes versus a roughly 4.5 million tonne PVC industry in fiscal 25 — about 5% — calling it a niche product today, confined mainly to hot-and-cold internal plumbing. Nothing in this passage touches the separation.
points.quote: It is about 2 and half lakh tons now.

points.point: Kairav Engineer said the real CPVC expansion depends on fire-sprinkler pipes, where Astral holds UL and local-body approvals, because a building uses more fire pipes than plumbing pipes; Sandeep Engineer added that standards changes are still needed.
points.quote: CPVC real value unlocking will happen when the ■re products pick up.

points.point: The Chemicals Business is described as having diversified across adhesives, PVA, cyanoacrylates, solvent cements, silicone sealants, epoxy resins, construction chemicals and putties, and scaled into specialty chemicals via recent acquisitions, all complementing Astral Chemie's existing paints and coatings business.
points.quote: The reorganisation will consolidate the Chemicals Business of Demerged Company  with the existing paints and coatings business of the Resulting Company  under a single, dedicated corporate platform managed by a focused leadership team with deep sector -specific expertise.

points.point: Size of the carve-out is quantified: the Demerged Undertaking turned over ₹12,663 million in FY26, 21% of Astral's total turnover (standalone FY26 turnover ₹59,076 million, net worth ₹41,058 million).
points.quote: The turnover of the Demerged Undertaking for the year ended March 31, 2026 stood at ₹  12,663 million .

points.point: Capital-allocation independence is the fourth stated principle: each business sets its own capex, working capital and funding according to its own capital intensity and cash-flow profile, and the demerger isolates each one's operational, cyclical and compliance risks.
points.quote: The reorganisation will enable each business to independently determine its capital expenditure, working- capital requirements, funding and investment strategies based on their respective growth prospects, capital intensity, cash- flow profile and risk -return characteristics.

points.point: Separate listing is justified as widening the investor and funding base rather than as an immediate valuation claim — no re-rating or multiple is asserted anywhere in the rationale.
points.quote:

have the flexibility, subject to Applicable Laws, to independently access debt and

points.point: Management teams are to be freed to run their own plans: independent capacity expansion, new products, new markets and their own bolt-on acquisitions and collaborations — the same language is repeated for the Al-Aziz amalgamation.
points.quote:
The reorganisation will enable the respective management teams to independently 
formulate and execute business plans, undertake capacity expansion, develop new 
products, enter new markets and pursue focused acquisitions, collaborations and other

points.point: The simultaneous amalgamation folds Al-Aziz Plastics (FY26 turnover ₹373 million, net worth ₹215 million; electrofusion and compression fittings, saddles, electrical fittings) into Astral's Plumbing Business, with compliance-cost reduction cited explicitly; its shares held by Astral are extinguished and it is dissolved without winding up.
points.quote: The amalgamation will enable the integration of its manufacturing facilities and capabilities, products, and customer relationships with the Plumbing Busi ness, while also reducing legal and regulatory compliances burden and related administrative costs.

points.point: Shareholders are kept whole on a mirror basis: 1-for-1 share issue at ₹1 face value, no cash consideration, no change in Astral's shareholding pattern, and Astral Chemie moving from 100% promoter-held to promoters 54.22% / public 45.78%, with NSE and BSE listing sought.

rationale.rationale: Apollo Hospitals Enterprise (the Demerged Company) today runs three verticals — Healthcare Services (hospitals), Apollo HealthCo (omnichannel pharmacy and digital health) and AHLL (diagnostics and primary care) — and is carving the omnichannel pharmacy/digital health business (the 'Identified Business Undertaking', carried on directly and through Apollo Healthco Ltd, 'Transferor Company 1') into a separately listed Resultant Company, referred to on the May 2026 call as Apollo Healthtech. Management confirmed in Aug 2025 that 'Apollo HealthCo., as you are seeing in the current form' is what gets demerged and listed, as part of a composite scheme that simultaneously amalgamates Keimed (Transferor Company 2) and AHL into the new entity, consolidating pharmacy distribution in 'an independent company focusing exclusively on digital health and pharmacy distribution.' The stated problem is strategic mismatch: the board says the business is 'distinct from other businesses undertaken by Demerged Company, and necessitates a differentiated strategy aligned to its industry specific risks, market dynamics, and growth trajectory,' so separation enables focus, efficient management and control, cost rationalization, streamlined statutory compliances and economies of scale for both sides. The capital-markets motive is explicit in the filing — the Resultant Company is to 'build a wider capital and financial base, by attracting a different set of investors, strategic partners, lenders and stakeholders' — i.e. a vehicle with its own shareholder base rather than a pharmacy/digital business funded inside a hospital company. Operationally they cite supply-chain integration, higher availability and larger assortment, and improved supply-chain transparency 'preventing the entry of counterfeit or substandard medicines.' The numbers management attached: a combined-entity run rate of INR 25,000 crore of revenue at 7% EBITDA (Feb 2026), Apollo HealthCo crossing INR 10,000 crore of annual revenue for the first time in FY26, a 3,200-crore GMV target with digital breakeven targeted in Q4 (Aug 2025), and management's view that 'the biggest lift' to EBITDA comes once the digital business breaks even. Incentive alignment is also built in: an Upside Agreement dated June 30, 2025 under which Rasmeli shares part of its investment upside with the AHL Promoter (Shobana Kamineni) and identified AHL employees 'in order to incentivise the management,' plus a reconstituted board (AHL Promoter, 3 Resultant-Company-promoter nominees, 1 AHEL nominee, 1 Rasmeli nominee, 6 independent directors).
rationale.evolution: By the Aug 2025 call the structure was already decided and analysts were asking for mechanics: Raman KV mapped the three segments and A. Krishnan confirmed Apollo HealthCo in its then-current form would be demerged and listed, with Keimed merging in for pharmacy synergies; the underlying Upside Agreement is dated June 30, 2025. By Feb 2026 the story had shifted from design to regulatory execution plus a hard financial target — CCI and SEBI approvals obtained, NCLT filed and hearings begun, Keimed's subsidiary network streamlined into 100% subsidiaries, and a stated combined run rate of INR 25,000 crore revenue at 7% EBITDA. In May 2026 management reframed it as a completed-year 'strategic restructuring of the omnichannel pharmacy and digital health business' for 'unlocking long-term value', set the NCLT-convened shareholder meeting for June 24, and reaffirmed (unchanged, 'as planned earlier') listing of Apollo Healthtech by end-December/early Q4 FY27, by which point the entity should show INR 25,000 crore of annualized revenue. Across the three calls the rationale itself never changed; only the timetable, approvals and the revenue milestones hardened.

points.point: Analyst Raman KV laid out the three-segment structure (hospitals, Apollo HealthCo pharmacy, AHLL diagnostics/primary care) and asked whether the pharmacy business was being demerged; A. Krishnan confirmed Apollo HealthCo in its current form is what gets demerged and listed.

points.point: Management reaffirmed the digital/pharmacy operating targets underpinning the separated entity: GMV of 3,200 on course per AOP, diagnostics at a 'new normal', and breakeven on course for Q4, with gross margin about 340 bps higher in Q1 vs Q4.
points.quote: So, the GM V of 3,200 that we spoke about, we continue to be on course.

points.point: Management tied the composite scheme (Keimed merger + Apollo HealthCo demerger) to a specific scale outcome for the combined entity: INR 25,000 crore of combined revenue at 7% EBITDA.
points.quote: We have also made progress with respect to the regulatory integration process for the com posite scheme of Keimed merger and demerger of Apollo HealthCo and remain well positioned to capture the full benefits of scale with the combined entity to achieve a run rate of INR 25,000 crore in combined revenues with 7% EBITDA.

points.point: Obul Reddy gave the regulatory status: CCI and SEBI approvals obtained, NCLT filing made and hearings started, with the next step awaited.

points.point: On the pre-condition that Keimed buy out associates holding stakes in the separate pieces, management said Keimed is on time and has consolidated the structure into wholly owned subsidiaries.

points.point: Management characterised the transaction in its own words as a strategic restructuring of the omnichannel pharmacy and digital health business aimed at sharpening focus and unlocking long-term value across the integrated platform.
points.quote: During the year, we also announced a strategic restructuring of the omnichannel pharmacy and digital health business, an important step towards sharpening focus on unlocking long -term value across our integrated health care platform.

points.point: Timeline reaffirmed: NCLT-convened shareholder meeting on June 24, demerger completion targeted by Q4 FY27, unchanged from the earlier plan.
points.quote: The NCLT convened meeting of the shareholders is now being called for on June 24 to obtain the requisite shareholder approval, consequent to which we are hopeful the demerger process is completed by Q4 FY27 as planned earlier.

points.point: Scale milestones cited for the business being separated: consolidated revenue crossed INR 25,000 crore (INR 25,229 crore) for the first time and Apollo HealthCo alone passed INR 10,000 crore in annual revenue, after Healthcare Services did so in FY25.
points.quote: Apollo HealthCo also surpassed INR 10,000 crore in annual revenues for the first time following a similar milestone achieved by our Healthcare Services business in FY25.

points.point: A. Krishnan named the listed entity and the listing window, and said it should show INR 25,000 crore of annualized revenue by that quarter.
points.quote: And hopefully, by Q4 FY27, end of December or early Q4 FY27 is when Apollo Healthtech should get demerged and listed.

points.point: Management said the decisive earnings driver for the separated entity is digital breakeven, with store/distribution maturation already visible and the cost structure supporting the growth; they claim to be on course versus published pro forma.
points.quote: But I think the biggest lift will come the moment the digital business breaks even and then starts contributing to the EBITDA story because if you have to look at the cost structure that is something which is reasonably and this growth should be able to su stain that.

points.point: The core board rationale: the Identified Business Undertaking is distinct from AHEL's other businesses and needs its own strategy for its industry-specific risks and growth trajectory, so both companies can focus, manage and control efficiently.
points.quote: The Scheme would enable carving-out of the Identified Business Undertaking (as defined in the Scheme) , which is distinct from other businesses undertaken by Demerged Company, and necessitates a differentiated strategy aligned to its industry specific risks, market dynamics, and growth trajectory.

points.point: The scheme consolidates the pharmacy distribution businesses of AHL (Transferor Company 1) and Keimed (Transferor Company 2) into one independent company focused exclusively on digital health and pharmacy distribution.
points.quote: The Scheme would also result in consolidation of pharmacy distribution business of Transferor Company 1 and Transferor Company 2, in an independent company focusing exclusively on digital health and pharmacy distribution, enabling synergies;

points.point: The explicit capital-markets purpose: a separate vehicle able to raise a wider capital and financial base by attracting a different investor, partner and lender set — the clearest statement of who the separation is for.
points.quote: The Scheme is expected to enable Resultant Company to build a wider capital and financial base, by attracting a different set of investors, strategic partners, lenders and stakeholders, as well as promoting overall business growth;

points.point: Operating benefits claimed include supply-chain integration with higher availability and larger assortment, and supply-chain transparency that keeps counterfeit or substandard medicines out of the ecosystem.
points.quote: Improved transparency in the supply chain preventing the entry of counterfeit or substandard medicines into the ecosystem;

points.point: Management incentives are embedded via the June 30, 2025 Upside Agreement: Rasmeli shares part of its investment upside with the AHL Promoter (Shobana Kamineni) and identified AHL employees, with the obligation re-linked to Rasmeli's shareholding in the Resultant Company.
points.quote: Rasmeli has agreed to share an agreed portion of the upside received by it (and its affiliates) pursuant to its investment into Transferor Company 1 with the AHL Promoter and the identified employees of Transferor Company 1 (or any successor entity), its (existing and future) subsidiaries and (existing and future) associate companies, in order to incentivise the management of such companies.

points.point: Governance of the new entity is pre-set: board of AHL Promoter, three Resultant-Company-promoter nominees, one AHEL nominee, one Rasmeli nominee and six independent directors; a rights issue of 9,95,50,000 shares for INR 19,91,00,000 is also provided for.
points.quote: Upon the Scheme becoming effective, the board of directors of Resultant Company shall be reconstituted as follows: (i) AHL Promoter; (ii) 3 (three) directors nominated by the Resultant Company Promoters; (iii) 1 (one) director nominated by Demerged Company; (iv) 1 (one) director nominated by Rasmeli; and (v) 6 (six) independent directors.

rationale.what_management_expects: Resultant Company (Apollo Healthtech): a pure digital-health and pharmacy-distribution vehicle at ~INR 25,000 crore annualized revenue and 7% EBITDA, with its own investors, partners and lenders, supply-chain integration, cost rationalization, scale economies, and EBITDA lift once digital breaks even. AHEL: focus on hospitals plus AHLL, sharper managerial and board attention, and long-term value unlocked across the platform.
rationale.gaps: No share entitlement ratio, valuation, debt or working-capital allocation, royalty/brand or supply agreements between entities, post-demerger hospital margins, Rasmeli's economics, or who first demanded separation.

rationale.rationale: Astra Microwave Products Limited (AMPL) is demerging its Space, Meteorology and Hydrology business into its wholly owned subsidiary Astra Space Technologies Private Limited (ASTPL), leaving AMPL as a Radar Electronics, Electronic Warfare and Telemetry focused entity — i.e. two sector-focused listed entities. Management framed the core problem as a conglomerate of unlike businesses under one roof: the company does design, development and manufacture of RF and microwave sub-systems across defence, space, meteorology and telecommunication, and the Space/Meteorology/Hydrology piece 'operates in a sector with distinct industry characteristics, competitive dynamics, regulatory environment, and risk profile, necessitating a differentiated growth strategy.' The separated unit is small relative to the parent: turnover of roughly INR 157 crores for FY ended 31 March 2026, 13.58% of total turnover (against group turnover of INR 1157 crores for FY26), so it was arguably starved of dedicated management attention inside a defence-led parent guiding 15–20% FY27 top-line growth. The stated fixes are sharper strategic and operational focus, dedicated management teams pursuing sector-specific growth opportunities, enhanced governance and accountability, a simplified corporate structure, and clearer investment propositions for shareholders. The filing is explicit that a standalone space entity 'would be better positioned to attract investors, strategic partners, lenders, and other stakeholders with sector-specific interests' — the demand cited is from capital providers and partners generally, not any named investor or lender. Mechanically it is a mirror demerger: 1 ASTPL share of INR 2 for every 1 AMPL share of INR 2, no cash consideration, ASTPL's existing 100% promoter-held capital cancelled, post-scheme shareholding 6.45% promoters / 93.55% public, to be listed on BSE and NSE, subject to NCLT, SEBI and exchange approvals. Management also tied the move to capitalizing on emerging opportunities in India and globally, and to value unlocking for shareholders.
rationale.evolution: In the passages supplied, the idea appears only at the Jun 2026 call (transcript dated May 27, 2026), where the Board had given in-principle approval to demerge the space, meteorology and hydrology business and management said the detailed scheme would be shared 'once it is formally approved by board, which is expected over the next few weeks.' That promise was kept on the stated timeline: the Board approved the Scheme of Arrangement on 10 June 2026, on the recommendation of the Independent Directors Committee and Audit Committee, with the filing dated 10.06.2026. So the only observable evolution is in-principle approval plus a qualitative rationale in May 2026, hardening weeks later into a formal scheme with the resulting entity named (ASTPL), the perimeter defined, turnover quantified (INR 157 crores / 13.58%), and a 1:1 share entitlement ratio. No earlier call passages discussing the separation were provided, so nothing can be said from these texts about whether the idea surfaced before May 2026.

rationale.what_management_expects: Each entity gets a dedicated management team and sector-fit strategy: AMPL concentrates on radar, EW and telemetry with 15–20% FY27 growth and rising R&D; ASTPL gets focused attention, tailored growth strategies and capital allocation, and better access to sector-specific investors, strategic partners and lenders. Group-wide: better capital allocation, improved operational efficiency, stronger governance and accountability, a simpler structure, clearer investment propositions, and value unlocking for shareholders.
rationale.gaps: No standalone margins, order book, assets, debt or employee split; no synergy/cost-of-separation estimate; no timeline to listing; no analyst Q&A or named investor pushing it.

judge.what_is_spun: HUL's Ice Cream Business Undertaking, demerged into Kwality Wall's (India) Limited, a pure-play India ice cream company
judge.reason: "Separation beneficial for both Companies" — tailoring the operating model for ice cream cold chain, and focusing investment algorithm and incentives to ice cream.
judge.insiders: Promoter/management stake not stated. HUL holders get 1 KWIL share per HUL share. HUL CFO Ritesh Tiwari is non-executive director; Prashant Premrajka executive director & CFO, Chitrank Goel deputy MD.
judge.hidden_value: A #2 India ice cream player with top-tier gross margins whose EBITDA collapsed from 7.1% (FY24-25) to 0.0% (H1 FY25-26) on cocoa, GST and standalone costs — with a margin-recovery roadmap in an 11%-growth market; parent gains 50-60bps margin.
judge.selling_pressure_why: 1-for-1 shares to every HUL holder of a small, currently zero-EBITDA pure-play cold-chain ice cream company; different industry from FMCG parent.
judge.listing_timeline: Oct 2025 call: "We expect to complete the demerger by December, with the listing anticipated in Quarter 4 of Financial Year 2026, subject to necessary regulatory approvals"; Feb 2026 call: "we have completed the demerger of the Ice Cream business this quarter".

rationale.rationale: The trigger was external to India: after parent Unilever PLC announced its intention to separate its ice cream business globally, HUL's Board ran a comprehensive review through an independent committee and decided to separate its own Ice Cream Business Undertaking. The stated business reason is structural mismatch — the scheme cites ice cream's "different operating model," including differentiated infrastructure for supply and distribution (cold chain), distinct capital allocation needs, and a distinct channel landscape and go-to-market strategy, which do not fit the rest of HUL's FMCG machine. Two routes were weighed on the Oct 2024 call — outright sale, or demerge and list — with the decision criteria explicitly stated as maximising shareholder value while minimising business disruption; HUL chose the demerger into Kwality Wall's (India) Limited (KWIL) on a 1:1 share entitlement ratio (Deloitte India Valuation LLP as registered valuer, Kotak Mahindra Capital fairness opinion), so every HUL shareholder directly owns the new listed ice cream company and can stay invested in its growth. Management sized the business as roughly 3% of HUL's turnover earning low single-digit EBITDA margins versus HUL's ~23%, so the carve-out mechanically lifts HUL's reported EBITDA margin by 50-60 bps (guidance 22-23% becomes an implied 22.5-23.5%), while Ritesh Tiwari argued the loss of 3% of turnover does not change HUL's scale at a kirana store. For the ice cream entity, the case is a focused, experienced, dedicated management team with flexibility to run a distinctive operating model, iconic brands (Kwality Wall's, Cornetto, Magnum) in an attractive high-growth category, and continued access to the portfolio, brand, innovation and technical expertise of the largest global ice cream business. For HUL, it is one of a sequence of portfolio-sharpening moves — divestment of atta and salt, divestment of the water business (Pureit, completed 1 Nov, unlocking circa Rs. 600 crores), and redeployment into high-growth demand spaces via Minimalist (turnover over Rs. 500 crores in FY25) and OZiva (Rs. 100 crores to Rs. 400 crores run rate; remaining 49% bought for Rs. 824 crores) — framed as 'fewer, bigger bets'. The scheme also claims a smoother transition for ice cream's people, and ring-fences ice cream creditors' claims onto the Resulting Company (with NCLT directing HUL to ensure KWIL can meet those obligations). Notably, no investor, lender, partner or regulator is named anywhere as having demanded the separation — the parent's global decision plus the Board's own review are the only sources given.
rationale.evolution: Oct 2024: following Unilever's global announcement, HUL confirms separation in principle but not the mode — an independent committee is weighing sale versus demerger-and-listing, with a route decision targeted by end of the calendar year, and ice cream sized at ~3% of business. Jan 2025: the Board approves the scheme of arrangement to demerge into Kwality Wall's (India) Limited at 1:1, with the detailed business rationale having been laid out at the Capital Markets Day, alongside the Pureit divestment and Minimalist acquisition. Apr 2025 and Oct 2025: execution-only updates — on track with regulatory requirements, completion by end-FY2026, then a specified two-step sequence (demerger in the December quarter with ice cream reported as discontinued, listing in Q4 FY26) plus the first explicit margin arithmetic of 50-60 bps. Feb 2026: demerger completed in the December quarter, with one-time non-cash demerger gain inside reported PAT of Rs. 6,603 crores (+121%), continuing-business EBITDA margin of 23.3%, KWIL listing on 16 February; by May 2026 it is cited retrospectively as a completed portfolio-rotation action already improving the growth mix.

rationale.rationale: Management says Lemon Tree Hotels has two businesses with fundamentally different economics bundled inside one listed company: an asset-heavy hotel ownership, leasing and development business, and an asset-light management, brand, loyalty, distribution and technology platform. Keswani laid out the economic spread explicitly in Aug 2025 — managing a hotel earns 17% of EBITDA, franchising 10%, leasing requires putting in 10%-20% of capital value for 50%-60% of EBITDA, and owning 100% means taking 100% of EBITDA with 100% of the risk — so under the Composite Scheme of Arrangement Fleur Hotels' mandate becomes building, buying or leasing hotels while Lemon Tree will only manage or franchise and 'will not lease hotels once the Fleur demerger happens.' A second stated problem is the balance sheet being misread: he complained analysts were 'blindly adding the lease liability' to compute debt-to-EBITDA, noting only 60%-65% of debt is bank debt and that continued leasing under Ind AS 116 would keep inflating lease liability and depreciation. The scheme fixes this by transferring all the debt, including Lemon Tree's own, to Fleur — about Rs. 1,300 crore against Fleur EBITDA of roughly Rs. 900 crore / $100 million next year, with Fleur then debating deploying another Rs. 1,300-1,400 crore — leaving Lemon Tree effectively debt-free with fee income available as free cash rather than being redeployed into capital (dividend policy to be decided by the Board within six months). The investor/partner dimension is central: Warburg Pincus has completed the purchase of APG's stake in Fleur, holds 26% fully diluted, and has a Rs. 960 crore commitment deployable only in the next 12 months, because once Fleur lists further capital must come from internal accruals or QIPs — and Warburg 'want to take a large stake in Fleur, put in 100's and 100's million dollars for a chunky return,' which Keswani says cannot be done against a ROFO inside the listed parent. Mechanically Lemon Tree transfers 17 hotels plus development capabilities and its shareholders receive Fleur shares, so they end up owning close to 74% of Fleur (33% direct, ~41% indirect) versus the 59% Lemon Tree owns directly today; the filing puts the retained stake at ~41.03%, subject to dilution from the Proposed Preferential Issue. The filing frames the purpose as segregating a 'distinct and self-sustaining undertaking' to achieve 'operational focus, greater flexibility for capital deployment, and clearer alignment of business objectives,' plus separate listing for 'transparent price discovery and market-driven valuation of the asset-heavy business,' a flexible structure to attract co-development partners without affecting brand operations or control, separate management teams and governance, and — via the amalgamation of two wholly owned subsidiaries into the Company — removal of legal layering, duplication, compliance costs and controllership overheads. Organizationally it was pre-wired: separate Managing Directors (Neelendra Singh for Lemon Tree from October 1, Saurabh for Fleur), with Keswani as Fleur's Executive Chair and ceasing his Lemon Tree executive role from March 2027.
rationale.evolution: It surfaced on the Aug 2025 call as an exploratory step — committees of directors had been set up in both Lemon Tree and Fleur to evaluate transferring assets from Lemon Tree into Fleur by demerger and then listing Fleur, with Keswani refusing to specify shareholding or the mechanism until those committees reported back, while the senior-management change (Neelendra from October 1, Keswani on an 18-month extension as Executive Director) was explicitly made so two people could run the two companies independently. On the Nov 2025 call it was only 'in process' with both boards and their subcommittees in discussion, Keswani promising 'a bunch of interesting things' within three months plus 'some other even more exciting stuff.' By the dedicated Jan 15, 2026 call the Composite Scheme of Arrangement was announced and the rationale became concrete — all debt to Fleur (~Rs. 1,300 crore), Lemon Tree at zero debt, Warburg at 26% fully diluted with Rs. 960 crore deployable in 12 months — and the Feb 2026 call added the consequences (Fleur targeting Rs. 1,000 crore EBITDA, Lemon Tree a net-cash company with a dividend policy due in six months). By Jun 2026 the structure was fixed and pro forma financials were published: Warburg had completed the APG purchase, 17 hotels plus development capabilities move to Fleur, shareholders end at ~74% of Fleur, and the timeline had slipped — CCI approval received in April, shareholder and SEBI approval pending before NCLT filing, with guidance moving from '12 months from Jan' to another 12-15 months, which Kapil Sharma characterized as a one-month delay on a conservative estimate.

points.point: First disclosure: committees of directors in both Lemon Tree and Fleur were set up to evaluate a demerger of assets from Lemon Tree into Fleur and then list Fleur, making Lemon Tree asset-light and Fleur a PropCo.
points.quote: So, the intent is that Lemon Tree will then become asset light, a significant shareholder in Fleur and will focus on management, brand and technology as a company, which is, I think , quite common to what have been global trends in this space.

points.point: The economic logic was spelled out as a fee-vs-capital split: 17% of EBITDA for management, 10% for franchising, 50%-60% for a lease requiring 10%-20% of capital value, 100% of EBITDA with 100% of risk for ownership — so Fleur takes capital-intensive activity and Lemon Tree takes only fees.
points.quote: Fleur's mandate will be to focus on, at the right value, building, buying, or leasing hotels. Lemon Tree's will only be to manage or franchise. Lemon Tree will not lease hotels once the Fleur demerger happens.

points.point: A stated problem is market misreading of leverage: analysts added lease liability into debt-to-EBITDA, when only 60%-65% of debt is bank debt and continued leasing under Ind AS 116 would keep inflating lease liability and depreciation.
points.quote: I noticed that some analysts were saying our debt -to-EBITDA is some very large number. And I think they were just blindly adding the lease liability.

points.point: Investors were already pressing on mechanics and value unlocking — how much of Fleur Lemon Tree would hold, whether shareholders get one-for-one shares — and management deferred to the two committees' recommendations to the boards.
points.quote: We have said a potential demerger. How will the demerger work is something that they have to come back with their recommendations to the board too.

points.point: Asked by Abhay Khaitan for process and timeline, management said the demerger was still with subcommittees and both full boards, and pre-announced news within three months — plus unspecified additional items.
points.quote: It is not only the demerger of Fleur, but some other even more exciting stuff, but we will talk about it when the time is right.

points.point: Opening remarks set the context as a structural upcycle the group had positioned for — Aurika Mumbai commissioned, a 500-plus room Aurika at Nehru Place secured, ~7,000 rooms signed under third-party management, ~130 hotels and ~11,700 rooms operating — making the reorganization the 'logical and value accretive next step' into two well-capitalized businesses with separate MDs already in place.
points.quote: The proposed reorganization will result in 2 distinct well-capitalized businesses, Lemon Tree Hotels as a pure -play asset -light company focused on offering hotel management, brand , loyalty distribution and digital services.

points.point: Debt is wholly reallocated: Fleur takes 100% of group debt including Lemon Tree's (~Rs. 1,300 crore at demerger) against ~Rs. 900 crore / $100 million EBITDA next year, with a further Rs. 1,300-1,400 crore of deployment under debate; Lemon Tree is left at zero debt.
points.quote: Firstly, when this demerger happens, all the debt, including the Lemon Tree's debt, after adjustment is being transferred to Fleur. Fleur will have 100% of our debt and Lemon Tree will have zero debt.

points.point: A capital partner is a driver: Warburg wants a large direct stake in Fleur and has Rs. 960 crore deployable only within 12 months, because once Fleur lists additional capital must come from internal accruals or QIPs; Warburg is at 26% fully diluted against Lemon Tree's 41%, and more money dilutes Lemon Tree.
points.quote: So, this is why they want to take a large stake in Fleur, put in 100 's and 100's million dollars for a chunky return.

points.point: Post-scheme Lemon Tree becomes net cash: all assets and debt go to Fleur, significant renovation spend (OPEX over Rs. 100 crore, CAPEX Rs. 70-80 crore) shrinks after FY27, and fee income becomes free cash rather than capital, with a dividend policy for the Board to decide in six months.
points.quote: Lemon Tree will immediately effectively be a debt -free company from next year. And all the fee income that it earns, which will be fairly significant, will therefore be not redeployed in capital, but will rather be available as free cash.

points.point: Growth is explicitly routed through Fleur post-demerger — greenfield, brownfield and outright acquisitions, including multiple opportunities totalling about 2,500 keys that would be rebranded rather than added as new brands — against the Rs. 1,000 crore Fleur EBITDA figure cited on the post-demerger call.
points.quote: And I am pretty sure that in the next 12 months, we will show a bunch of additions. Some may be greenfield, some may be brownfield and some may be outright acquisitions.

points.point: Final mechanics with pro forma financials published: Warburg completed the APG purchase, Lemon Tree transfers 17 hotels plus development capabilities, shareholders receive Fleur shares and Fleur lists, lifting shareholders' Fleur economics from 59% held via Lemon Tree to ~74% (33% direct, ~41% indirect) before any Warburg primary infusion — delivered against FY26 revenue of Rs. 1,452.7 crore (up 13%) and net EBITDA of Rs. 699.3 crore (up 10%).
points.quote: Next, Lemon Tree will transfer 17 hotels and development capabilities in exchange for which Lemon Tree shareholders will get Fleur shares, leading to Fleur's listing as a separate entity.

points.point: Continuity is preserved by long-term management agreements that give Lemon Tree stable, growing fee income from Fleur and let Fleur underwrite deals faster, with Fleur's hotels fully renovated by demerger; Keswani becomes Fleur's Executive Chair and leaves his Lemon Tree executive role from March 2027. Timeline slipped: CCI approval in April, shareholder and SEBI approval pending before NCLT, guidance now 12-15 months versus the earlier 12 months, described as about a one-month delay.
points.quote: Post reorganization, Lemon Tree will emerge as a debt -free, high-margin, high ROCE company generating strong free cash flows from fees and brand -related income.

points.point: The filing states a detailed review concluded the asset-heavy hotel-ownership plus Development Capabilities business is a distinct, self-sustaining undertaking better housed in the Transferee Company (in which the Company holds 58.91%), with the stated aims of operational focus, capital-deployment flexibility and alignment of objectives, retaining unified strategic control while granting each entity operational independence and financial flexibility.
points.quote: Therefore, to achieve operational focus, greater flexibility for capital deployment, and clearer alignment of business objectives, it is proposed under this Scheme to (i) amalgamate Transferor Company 3, Transferor Company 4, Transferor Company 5 and Transferor Company 6 with the Transferee Company;  and (ii) demerge and vest the Demerged Undertaking (comprising the Demerged Hotel Properties and the Development Capabilities together with the related undertakings, as defined hereinafter) into the Transferee C ompany, while the Company will continue to focus on the asset -light hotel management support, brand and operations including management support of the hotels transferred to the Transferee Company and other properties.

points.point: Separate listing is justified as giving direct shareholder participation plus independent valuation and capital access — the Transferee ceases to be a subsidiary, the Company retains ~41.03% subject to dilution from the Proposed Preferential Issue — alongside a flexible structure to attract investors or co-development partners for specific projects without affecting brand operations or control, separate management teams and governance frameworks, and simplification via merging two wholly owned subsidiaries to cut layering, duplication, compliance costs and controllership overheads.
points.quote: Following the implementation of the Scheme, the Transferee Company will cease to be a subsidiary of the Company , and its shares will be listed on the Stock Exchanges, enabling transparent price discovery and market -driven valuation of the asset -heavy business.

rationale.what_management_expects: Lemon Tree: pure-play asset-light management, brand, loyalty, distribution and digital business — zero debt from next year, high margin, high ROCE, strong free cash from fees, hypercharged franchising/soft brand, dividend policy pending. Fleur: large-scale growth-oriented ownership/leasing PropCo with in-house development, ~Rs. 1,300 crore debt against ~Rs. 900-1,000 crore EBITDA, Warburg capital, listed valuation and price discovery. Both: accountability, focus, value unlocking.
rationale.gaps: No share-entitlement ratio or valuation basis for the demerger itself, no tax treatment, no specific management-fee rates to Fleur, no dividend policy, no listing-date value estimate.

rationale.rationale: The separation is a demerger of the "Clinical Services" undertaking (the primary/secondary care clinics NHIC runs across Bengaluru) out of NH Integrated Care Private Limited (NHIC) and into the listed parent Narayana Hrudayalaya Limited (NHL), with an Appointed Date of April 1, 2025. Management's stated reason is that the clinics turned out not to be standalone: NHIC was incorporated to run primary and secondary care clinics "independently of hospital-based tertiary care services," but operational experience showed "substantial dependencies on hospital infrastructure" — consultant doctors and specialists primarily engaged at hospitals, advanced diagnostics "not viable at individual clinic locations," and patient pathways requiring tertiary care. Running clinics separately from hospitals forced duplicate administrative functions (finance, HR, procurement, IT, marketing), producing "increased costs, coordination inefficiencies, and the inability to realise economies of scale," and it crowded out NHIC's strategic priority, preventive healthcare. What stays behind in NHIC is Narayana Aarogyam, a preventive platform (health screening, risk assessment, wellness coaching, continuous monitoring) that is said to be structurally hospital-independent: dedicated technology-enabled testing centres, appointment-based services with no on-call specialists or emergency capability, minimal hospitalisation, and predictable resource needs — so it can go digital-first, AI-powered and asset-light, hire specialised digital health talent and pursue population-health partnerships. The filing cites "demonstrated investor interest in technology-enabled preventive healthcare platforms," plus lifestyle disease prevalence and corporate wellness mandates, as the growth case; no lender or partner demand is mentioned. The clinics being moved are small — Rs 39.94 crore of FY25 revenue, 1.11% of NHL's standalone turnover — and the mechanics are neutral: NHIC is already a wholly owned subsidiary, so there is no cash consideration, no share issuance, no change in shareholding and no new listing. On the June 2026 call Viren Shetty tied it directly to the clinic cash burn: sharing corporate overheads with the parent and "demerging the clinic business into the core" is how they expect to moderate costs while still expanding clinics, which they value as a patient feeder generating inpatient referrals for advanced therapies and future One Health insurance subscribers.
rationale.evolution: Of the passages supplied, the Feb 2026 call does not touch this transaction at all — it discusses a different restructuring, the UK Practice Plus carve-out (three legal entities, ~INR 40 crore depreciation for two months, with Sandhya J advising investors to wait for a full quarter). The clinic demerger first surfaces in the supplied material on the Jun 2026 call, where Viren Shetty mentions it almost in passing, as the answer to a question about continuing clinic cash burn: consolidation, shared corporate overheads with the parent, and "demerging the clinic business into the core." The scheme filing then formalises and broadens that same logic — hospital dependency, duplicated admin functions, value unlocking — and reframes the purpose around what remains in NHIC, the Aarogyam preventive healthcare platform, backdated to an Appointed Date of April 1, 2025 (i.e. before either call). No earlier call in the material contains the idea, so its origin and the preventive-healthcare framing appear only in the filing, not in the call record provided.

points.point: Viren Shetty frames the demerger as a cost/overhead fix: clinics move into the parent ("the core") so corporate overheads and resources are shared rather than duplicated, which is his answer to persistent clinic cash burn.
points.quote: What we are doing is a little bit of consolidation and a few of the corporate overheads can be worked in a way that we share resources with the parent and we'll be demerging the clinic business into the core that should help with a lot of that.

points.point: Management says clinic cash burn will continue at a similar run rate into the next year because they keep adding clinics, though fixed-cost leverage should moderate some of it — the pressure the restructuring is meant to relieve.
points.quote: So you have to assume that a similar run rate of cash burn will continue on the clinics going into next year as well because we still have a significant ambition in terms of growth of clinics in our core geographies.

points.point: The strategic justification for keeping clinics inside the hospital company: they reach domestic patients who would never otherwise come to Narayana, and feed inpatient referrals for advanced therapies and future One Health insurance customers.
points.quote: So they act as an excellent feeder for all the hospitals and build up that long -term relationship for patients who tomorrow will subscribe to our One Health plans insurance plans and then become Narayana Health customers.

points.point: This call addresses a separate restructuring, the UK Practice Plus carve-out, not the clinic demerger: Sandhya J explains that Practice Plus's old balance sheet covered three legal entities and the reported numbers are post-carve-out, with lease re-accounting agreed with the statutory auditors.
points.quote: So , the Practice Plus balance sheet was three legal entities which were there , and this is now after the carve out.

points.point: On the UK numbers (c. INR 40 crore depreciation for two months, per Slide 14), management tells investors the figures are usable going forward but to wait for a full quarter before treating them as representative.
points.quote: I would just recommend that you wait for Q4, where we get the full effect of all the numbers in our P&L.

points.point: Core operational reason: NHIC was set up to run clinics independently of hospital-based tertiary care, but experience showed the clinics depend on hospital-based specialists, hospital-grade diagnostics and tertiary care pathways.
points.quote: Operational experience has demonstrated  that the Demerged Undertaking has developed substantial dependencies on hospital infrastructure, particularly: (a) consultant doctors and specialists primarily engaged at hospital facilities; (b) advanced diagnostic services not viable at individual clinic locations; and (c) patient care pathways requiring tertiary care at hospital facilities.

points.point: Running clinics in a separate company duplicated finance, HR, procurement, IT and marketing, raising costs and blocking economies of scale, and distracted NHIC from its preventive healthcare priority.
points.quote: Separate operation of clinics and hospitals has necessitated duplicate administrative functions (finance, HR, procurement, IT, marketing), resulting in increased costs, coordination inefficiencies, and the inability to realise economies of scale.

points.point: Size and mechanics: the clinics being transferred had FY25 revenue of Rs 39.94 crore, 1.11% of NHL's standalone turnover; because NHIC is wholly owned, there is no cash, no share issue, no shareholding change and no new listing. Appointed Date is April 1, 2025.
points.quote: The turnover of the Clinical Services undertaking of the Demerged Company for the year ended March 31, 2025 was  Rs. 39.94 crore representing 1.11 % of the total standalone turnover of the Resulting Company for the year ended  March 31, 2025.

points.point: What remains in NHIC is Narayana Aarogyam — screening, risk assessment, wellness coaching and continuous monitoring — which is described as structurally independent of hospitals: appointment-based, no on-call specialists or emergency capability, minimal hospitalisation, predictable resource needs.
points.quote: Aarogyam operates independently of hospital infrastructure through: (a) dedicated technology-enabled preventive testing ce ntres; (b) scheduled appointment-based services without requiring on-call specialists or emergency capabilities; (c) minimal hospitalisation rates; and (d) predictable resource requirements without treatment-based operational variability.

points.point: Market/demand case, including the only reference to outside parties wanting this: investor appetite for technology-enabled preventive healthcare platforms, alongside lifestyle disease prevalence, corporate wellness mandates and digital health advances.
points.quote: The preventive healthcare sector presents  significant growth opportunities from lifestyle disease prevalence, corporate wellness mandates, technological advancements in digital health, and demonstrated investor interest in technology-enabled preventive healthcare platforms.

points.point: Post-demerger NHIC becomes a focused preventive-health company: digital-first and AI-powered, asset-light and scalable, with partnerships for population health management, and freedom to recruit specialised digital health expertise.

points.quote: The Demerged Undertaking and Remaining Un dertaking represent distinct business models with materially different value propositions, operating models, risk profiles, capital requirements, and growth drivers.

points.point: Capital allocation is explicitly split: NHIC funds preventive healthcare technology without competing demands, while NHL funds clinic infrastructure off its own balance sheet.
points.quote: The Demerged Company can direct capital toward preventive healthcare technology investments without competing demands.  The Resulting Company will fund clinic infrastructure from its capital base.

points.point: Claimed benefits include value unlocking and better valuations, improved patient care coordination, clearer employee career paths, and cleaner governance/regulatory boundaries; NHL also gains unified care pathways and optimised specialist deployment.
points.quote: The Scheme will: (a) unlock value from distinct business segments and enable enhanced valuations; (b) improve patient care coordination and service quality;  (c) establish clearer organisational structur es and career paths for employees; and  (d) establish clear operational boundaries for governance and regulatory compliance.

rationale.what_management_expects: NHL: clinics folded into the core — unified care pathways, optimised specialist deployment, consolidated admin, procurement/IT/working-capital savings, overheads shared with the parent moderating clinic cash burn, plus a patient feeder into hospitals and One Health insurance. NHIC: pure preventive-care play on Aarogyam — sharper focus, digital/AI asset-light capital allocation, specialised hiring, ecosystem partnerships, value unlocked and "enhanced valuations" for both segments.
rationale.gaps: Calls never quantify cost savings, Aarogyam's revenue or burn, the Rs 39.94 crore clinics, timelines or approvals; no investor, lender or partner named as requesting it.

The only profitability datum touching the clinics is combined: 'EBITDA for NHIC and NHIL stood at INR -674 Mn for FY26' (clinics plus insurance together), and Q1 FY27 shows only a blended 'EBITDA% of India Hospitals and NHIC Clinics together'. Neither is a clinic-only figure, so operating_profit is left null. Note also that the 'discontinued operations' in the FY25/FY26 consolidated accounts (revenue ₹1,342.25 Mn FY25, ₹1,377.37 Mn FY26) is the Jammu unit, not the clinic business.

judge.what_is_spun: Vedanta's power generation assets into Talwandi Sabo Power Ltd ("Vedanta Power"), alongside aluminium, oil & gas, iron & steel demergers
demerged_business_names: merchant power business of Vedanta Limited
judge.reason: To create focused, pure-play sector companies that unlock long-term value through sharper strategic focus, independent capital allocation and governance, simplifying Vedanta's structure and giving investors direct exposure to sector-leading assets.
judge.insiders: Promoter/management stake in the new entity not stated; shareholders of Vedanta Limited receive shares in each of the four resulting listed entities in proportion to existing holdings, ensuring continuity of ownership.
judge.hidden_value: Oil & gas entity MEL's net worth is projected to rise from negative INR 178 crores to positive INR 13,507 crores upon demerger, while that entity also absorbs large uncrystallised GoI claims (counterclaim of 8,596.80 crores).
judge.selling_pressure_why: Four new sector-specific entities distributed pro-rata to all VEDL holders; index treatment and float size not stated in documents.
judge.listing_timeline: Nov 2025 call: "This will set the stage for the listing of all five demerged entities by the end of FY '26"; Jan 2026 call: NCLT approved the scheme on 16 December 2025, certified copy received 21 January 2026, "targeting 1st of April"; power demerger approval still pending in a separate NCLT proceeding, and listing is subject to further regulatory and stock exchange approvals.
judge.read_next: The separate NCLT proceeding on the merchant power demerger, plus TSPL's share-entitlement ratio and net-worth certificate in the Scheme.
judge.quote: Shareholders of Vedanta Limited will receive equity shares in each of the four resulting listed entities (in addition to their shareholding in Vedanta Limited) in proportion to their existing holdings, ensuring continuity of ownership while enabling direct participation in the growth trajectories of individual businesses.

rationale.rationale: Management framed the separation as a value-unlocking restructuring: in the Nov 2023 call Arun Misra said the Board had approved demerging Vedanta Ltd. into six independent listed entities, 'each one capable of executing its individual business strategies,' with the scheme filed with the stock exchanges in October 2023 and described as creating 'six incredibly competitive, nimble and focused enterprises.' The scheme rationale gives the core logic: each demerged entity gets greater strategic flexibility, sharper market focus and independent access to capital, with management teams aligning decisions to customer needs, investment cycles and commodity-specific dynamics, while investors can 'evaluate and value each business on its own merits' — shareholders receive shares in proportion to existing holdings so ownership continuity is preserved. The resulting companies are Vedanta Aluminium (integrated aluminium, value-added and low-carbon), Vedanta Oil & Gas (via Malco Energy Ltd — India's largest private E&P), Vedanta Power (TSPL and other IPP assets), Vedanta Iron & Steel, and a base metals entity (Vedanta Base Metals Ltd), with the residual Vedanta Limited keeping the Hindustan Zinc stake and acting as 'an incubator for new and emerging businesses.' Chairman Anil Agarwal said each entity 'has the potential to grow manifold, attract strategic investment, and deliver superior value as these sectors are witnessing double digit growth,' and that the demerger is 'also about empowering leadership.' Management repeatedly tied it to scale and leadership depth — Aug 2024 cited '100-plus expats and experienced specialists' ready to run the separate businesses, and Nov 2024/Apr 2025 linked it to leadership in critical minerals and 'Vedanta 2.0' (global leader in critical minerals, energy transition and technology). Valuation was the explicit prize: in Nov 2024 Ajay Goel said 'there is a preponderance of opinion where everybody believes post-de-merger the value of the sums will be the parts will be more than the sum,' and promoter stake (VRL at 56.4% of VEDL) was expected to be worth more after the split. Creditors and regulators were active parties rather than requesters: the company was 'in talks with creditors for debt allocations' (Jan 2024), paid a Rs. 660 crore full-and-final SEPCO settlement 'as part of demerger proceedings' and a Rs. 1,248 crore bank guarantee to NCLAT over the TSPL demerger, and MoPNG/DGH objected over disputed Cairn dues. Throughout, the demerger was presented alongside deleveraging (VRL debt cut $3.7bn over two years, down to $5.5bn, targeting $3bn by 2027) and operating performance (FY25 revenue Rs. 150,725 crores, EBITDA Rs. 43,541 crores, net debt/EBITDA improved to 1.2x) as one of three priorities: 'business delivery, deleveraging, and demerger.'
rationale.evolution: The idea surfaced as a board decision in the Nov 2023 call — six independent listed entities, scheme filed with exchanges in October 2023 — and the Jan 2024 call tracked approvals (exchange NOC passed to SEBI, awaiting SEBI NOC, creditor talks on debt allocation) while loosely describing a future 'portfolio of 17 pure-play companies.' Through Aug 2024 and Nov 2024 it moved to NCLT (first hearing done), with management calling it 'a final step,' stressing scheme flexibility to list each entity as its approval came, and guiding completion 'on or before 31st of March 2025.' Feb 2025 set the shareholder/creditor meeting for Feb 18, which voted in favour, after which Apr 2025 moved to the second motion petition with completion guided to September 2025; the Jul 2025 call slipped that to a Sept–Oct window amid an NCLAT interim stay on the TSPL power demerger and MoPNG objections over Cairn's disputed dues. By the Oct 2025 call the count had become five demerged entities with a final NCLT hearing on November 12 and listing targeted by end-FY26, the SEPCO dispute settled for Rs. 660 crores to clear the path; the NCLT order was pronounced 16.12.2025.

points.point: The stated objective was restated as pure-play entities with better strategic focus and operational flexibility, in a year of record revenue of Rs. 150,725 crores, EBITDA of Rs. 43,541 crores and net debt/EBITDA improving to 1.2x from 1.5x.
points.quote: We are making good progress Vedanta Limited April 30, 2025 Page 4 of 22 Sensitivity: Internal (C3) with our demerger plan, aiming to create pure -play entities that will enhance strategic focus and operational flexibility.
